It was in the township of Dunwich, in a large and partly inhabited
farmhouse set against a hillside four miles from the village and a mile
and a half from any other dwelling, that Wilbur Whateley was born at 5
a. m. on Sunday, the second of February, 1913. This date was recalled
because it was Candlemas, which people in Dunwich curiously observe
under another name; and because the noises in the hills had sounded,
and all the dogs of the countryside had barked persistently, throughout
the night before. Less worthy of notice was the fact that the mother
was one of the decadent Whateleys, a somewhat deformed, unattractive
albino woman of 35, living with an aged and half-insane father
about whom the most frightful tales of wizardry had been whispered
in his youth. Lavinia Whateley had no known husband, but according
to the custom of the region made no attempt to disavow the child;
concerning the other side of whose ancestry the country folk might--and
did--speculate as widely as they chose. On the contrary, she seemed
strangely proud of the dark, goatish-looking infant who formed such a
contrast to her own sickly and pink-eyed albinism, and was heard to
mutter many curious prophecies about its unusual powers and tremendous
future.

Lavinia was one who would be apt to mutter such things, for she was a
lone creature given to wandering amidst thunderstorms in the hills and
trying to read the great odorous books which her father had inherited
through two centuries of Whateleys, and which were fast falling to
pieces with age and worm-holes. She had never been to school, but was
filled with disjointed scraps of ancient lore that Old Whateley had
taught her. The remote farmhouse had always been feared because of Old
Whateley's reputation for black magic, and the unexplained death by
violence of Mrs. Whateley when Lavinia was twelve years old had not
helped to make the place popular. Isolated among strange influences,
Lavinia was fond of wild and grandiose daydreams and singular
occupations; nor was her leisure much taken up by household cares in a
home from which all standards of order and cleanliness had long since
disappeared.

There was a hideous screaming which echoed above even the hill noises
and the dogs' barking on the night Wilbur was born, but no known doctor
or midwife presided at his coming. Neighbors knew nothing of him till
a week afterward, when Old Whateley drove his sleigh through the snow
into Dunwich Village and discoursed incoherently to the group of
loungers at Osborn's general store. There seemed to be a change in the
old man--an added element of furtiveness in the clouded brain which
subtly transformed him from an object to a subject of fear--though he
was not one to be perturbed by any common family event. Amidst it all
he showed some trace of the pride later noticed in his daughter, and
what he said of the child's paternity was remembered by many of his
hearers years afterward.

"I dun't keer what folks think--ef Lavinny's boy looked like his pa, he
wouldn't look like nothin' ye expeck. Ye needn't think the only folks
is the folks hereabouts. Lavinny's read some, an' has seed some things
the most o' ye only tell abaout. I calc'late her man is as good a
husban' as ye kin find this side of Aylesbury; an' ef ye knowed as much
abaout the hills as I dew, ye wouldn't ast no better church weddin' nor
her'n. Let me tell ye suthin'--_some day yew folks'll hear a child o'
Lavinny's a-callin' its father's name on the top o' Sentinel Hill!_"

The only persons who saw Wilbur during the first month of his life
were old Zechariah Whateley, of the undecayed Whateleys, and Earl
Sawyer's common-law wife, Mamie Bishop. Mamie's visit was frankly one
of curiosity, and her subsequent tales did justice to her observations;
but Zechariah came to lead a pair of Alderney cows which Old Whateley
had bought of his son Curtis. This marked the beginning of a course of
cattle-buying on the part of small Wilbur's family which ended only
in 1928, when the Dunwich horror came and went; yet at no time did
the ramshackle Whateley barn seem over-crowded with livestock. There
came a period when people were curious enough to steal up and count
the herd that grazed precariously on the steep hillside above the old
farmhouse, and they could never find more than ten or twelve anemic,
bloodless-looking specimens. Evidently some blight or distemper,
perhaps sprung from the unwholesome pasturage or the diseased fungi
and timbers of the filthy barn, caused a heavy mortality amongst the
Whateley animals. Odd wounds or sores, having something of the aspect
of incisions, seemed to afflict the visible cattle; and once or twice
during the earlier months certain callers fancied they could discern
similar sores about the throats of the gray, unshaven old man and his
slatternly, crinkly-haired albino daughter.

In the spring after Wilbur's birth Lavinia resumed her customary
rambles in the hills, bearing in her misproportioned arms the swarthy
child. Public interest in the Whateleys subsided after most of the
country folk had seen the baby, and no one bothered to comment on the
swift development which that newcomer seemed every day to exhibit.
Wilbur's growth was indeed phenomenal, for within three months of his
birth he had attained a size and muscular power not usually found in
infants under a full year of age. His motions and even his vocal sounds
showed a restraint and deliberateness highly peculiar in an infant,
and no one was really unprepared when, at seven months, he began to
walk unassisted, with falterings which another month was sufficient to
remove.

It was somewhat after this time--on Hallowe'en--that a great blaze was
seen at midnight on the top of Sentinel Hill where the old table-like
stone stands amidst its tumulus of ancient bones. Considerable talk
was started when Silas Bishop--of the undecayed Bishops--mentioned
having seen the boy running sturdily up that hill ahead of his mother
about an hour before the blaze was remarked. Silas was rounding up a
stray heifer, but he nearly forgot his mission when he fleetingly spied
the two figures in the dim light of his lantern. They darted almost
noiselessly through the underbrush, and the astonished watcher seemed
to think they were entirely unclothed. Afterward he could not be sure
about the boy, who may have had some kind of a fringed belt and a pair
of dark blue trunks or trousers on. Wilbur was never subsequently seen
alive and conscious without complete and tightly buttoned attire, the
disarrangement or threatened disarrangement of which always seemed to
fill him with anger and alarm. His contrast with his squalid mother and
grandfather in this respect was thought very notable until the horror
of 1928 suggested the most valid of reasons.

The next January gossips were mildly interested in the fact that
"Lavinny's black brat" had commenced to talk, and at the age of only
eleven months. His speech was somewhat remarkable both because of its
difference from the ordinary accents of the region, and because it
displayed a freedom from infantile lisping of which many children of
three or four might well be proud. The boy was not talkative, yet when
he spoke he seemed to reflect some elusive element wholly unpossessed
by Dunwich and its denizens. The strangeness did not reside in what he
said, or even in the simple idioms he used; but seemed vaguely linked
with his intonation or with the internal organs that produced the
spoken sounds. His facial aspect, too, was remarkable for its maturity;
for though he shared his mother's and grandfather's chinlessness, his
firm and precociously shaped nose united with the expression on his
large, dark, almost Latin eyes to give him an air of quasi-adulthood
and well-nigh preternatural intelligence. He was, however, exceedingly
ugly despite his appearance of brilliancy; there being something almost
goatish or animalistic about his thick lips, large-pored, yellowish
skin, coarse crinkly hair, and oddly elongated ears. He was soon
disliked even more decidedly than his mother and grandsire, and all
conjectures about him were spiced with references to the bygone magic
of Old Whateley, and how the hills once shook when he shrieked the
dreadful name of _Yog-Sothoth_ in the midst of a circle of stones with
a great book open in his arms before him. Dogs abhorred the boy, and
he was always obliged to take various defensive measures against their
barking menace.

In Dunwich township, in a great weather-warped farmhouse that clung to a hillside four miles from the village and a mile and a half from any other roof-light, Wilbur Whateley came into the world at five o’clock on a Sunday morning—the second of February, 1913. Folks remembered it not because new life had entered an old house, but because it was Candlemas, which Dunwich keeps by a name older than the meetinghouse ever heard; and because, all through the night before, the hills kept making their peculiar sounds and every dog in the countryside set up a ceaseless, furious barking—as if the ridges themselves were speaking in a tongue that made an animal’s blood bristle.

Domestic things went on in their usual poor order. The stove would have been banked with last night’s ash and half-burnt hardwood, the iron kettle sweating a thin steam that smelled of old beans and sour tin, and whatever bread there was would have been yesterday’s, hard at the heel and streaked with flour that never quite turned to dough. Yet the air of that house could not hold only homely odors. The place had long been full of a damp, cellarish taint—the rot of worm-shot beams, the rankness of mould rising from dirt floors, and a faint ammonia from the barn that the wind pushed through broken panes. Even when you thought you caught something as innocent as smoke or milk, it was cut with that other savor—like a book kept too long in a peat bog.

Wilbur’s mother was Lavinia Whateley—one of the decadent Whateleys: a white, deformed, unattractive albino woman of thirty-five with pink eyes that watered in strong light. She lived there with her father, old Whateley—aged, half-insane, and marked in the memories of Dunwich by the ugliest whispers of wizardry from his youth. Lavinia had no known husband; but in that countryside, where names and kin were weighed by gossip as much as by the Bible, she made no denial of the child. People speculated freely about the other half of the ancestry, and Lavinia did nothing to stop them. If anything, she was oddly proud of the dark, goatish-looking infant—so shocking against her own sickly pallor—and she was heard muttering prophecies over him as if he were a loaf rising in a warm corner, sure to swell beyond the pan and split the crust.

She was a lone creature who wandered in thunderstorms, climbing where the wind had the clearest voice and the trees clacked like dry bones. She had the habit of trying to read the great odorous books her father had inherited through two centuries of Whateleys—books so old their leather had turned to a greasy bitterness and their pages broke at a touch, tunnelled through by worms. Lavinia had never been to school, but she carried in her head disjointed scraps of ancient lore old Whateley had fed her, as one might feed a child scraps of salted meat and hard cheese from the table—enough to keep life in, not enough to make wholesome growth.

The farmhouse had always been feared, and not only because of old Whateley’s name. When Lavinia was twelve, Mrs. Whateley had died violently in a manner that no one ever got a plain account of, and that kind of silence is a spice sharper than pepper in a town’s talk. Standards of cleanliness had long since fallen away from the place. The floorboards were filmed; the table was sticky; crockery sat with gray rings of old porridge dried to stone; and the very air seemed to have been cooked too long, until it thickened. Lavinia did not trouble herself with household cares, and the kitchen—if it could be called that—held none of the comforting order that a decent farmwife keeps: no bright crocks, no neat strings of herbs, no jars of summer fruit shining like stained glass in winter. It was a poor larder in a poor house, as if the family fed on something other than honest food.

On the night Wilbur was born there was a screaming that rose above even the hill noises and the dog-barking—a hideous, tearing sound that did not belong to childbirth as Dunwich understood it. No doctor came; no midwife’s practiced hands were there. The nearest neighbors lay in their beds listening and trying not to listen, the way people do when they fear the sound might choose them next.

A week afterward, old Whateley drove his sleigh through the snow into Dunwich Village. At Osborn’s general store—where men lounged with their boots close to the stove and the smell of molasses, kerosene, and wet wool hung in the rafters—he discoursed incoherently. There was a change in him: more furtive, as if his clouded brain had shifted him from being merely a thing to fear into a mind that meant to do the fearing back. He was not the kind to be disturbed by common family events; yet amid his babble there was a pride like a knife-edge, and what he said about the child’s paternity stayed in the listeners’ minds for years, returning like a refrain whenever the hills made their odd sounds.

“I dun’t keer what folks think—ef Lavinny’s boy looked like his pa, he wouldn’t look like nothin’ ye expeck. Ye needn’t think the only folks is the folks hereabouts. I calc’late her man is as good a husban’ as ye kin find this side of Aylesbury; an’ ef ye knowed as much abaout the hills as I dew, ye wouldn’t ast no better church weddin’ nor her’n. Perhaps it was the way the old dialect strained around a name that wasn’t made for human mouths—like trying to say foreign spices with a tongue raised on salt pork. Perhaps it was the way the store’s familiar clatter—tin scoop in the cracker barrel, stove door creaking, boots scraping the planks—seemed suddenly too small and petty against whatever the old man was dragging in with him from the hills.

The hillside pasture above it held at most ten or twelve anemic, bloodless-looking beasts, grazing as if the grass were not grass but something tasteless they chewed out of habit.

Once or twice, in the earlier months, certain callers fancied they could make out similar marks about the throats of the gray, unshaven old man and his slatternly, crinkly-haired albino daughter. Interest in the Whateleys subsided once most of the country folk had had a look at the baby. No one cared to speak too long about what was unpleasant, and besides, there were plantings to see to, butter to churn, smokehouses to mend. Yet the uncanny threaded itself through the ordinary, as it always does in places where the land is old and the speech older. While women scalded pans and men sharpened scythes, Wilbur grew.

His growth was phenomenal. Within three months he had the size and muscular power not usually found in infants under a full year. His motions—his very sounds—had a restraint and deliberateness that made onlookers uneasy, as if he were tasting the world rather than merely crying at it. When, at seven months, he began to walk unassisted, people were not truly surprised; and within another month he had lost the faltering. It was as if time fed him too richly, over-proofing him past what nature intended, like dough left too long where it’s warm.

Somewhat after that—on Hallowe’en—a great blaze was seen at midnight on the top of Sentinel Hill, where the old table-like stone stands amid its tumulus of ancient bones. The sight set talk going from kitchen to store to barn, carried by the same mouths that traded recipes and seed corn. Silas had been rounding up a stray heifer, lantern swinging, and he nearly forgot his errand when he caught that glimpse in the underbrush. About the boy he wasn’t sure; maybe there’d been some kind of fringed belt, and a pair of dark blue trunks or trousers.

From then on, Wilbur was never seen alive and conscious without complete, tightly buttoned attire. The slightest disarrangement, or even the threat of it, filled him with anger and alarm. That was notable, because his mother and grandfather went as they pleased in their squalor, indifferent to rips and stains; but on Wilbur, clothes were not comfort or pride—they were necessity. It made people wonder, and in later years, when they had learned what came in 1928, they would remember the boy’s buttoned collars and stiff concealments and feel sick at how plain the answer had been.

It was different from the ordinary accents of the region, and it lacked the infant lisping that even children of three or four can’t always shed. He did not chatter. But when he spoke, there was an elusive element that Dunwich and its denizens did not possess. It wasn’t in the words themselves, nor even in the simple idioms; it was in the sound—his intonation, the shape of breath and throat behind it, as if the organs that made the voice were set differently than a human’s ought to be. In a place where people judged one another by how they said corn, how they said creek, how they said home, that difference was a wound in the ear. Their native dialect—already a dwindling thing, already mocked by outsiders and softened by printed schoolbooks—met in Wilbur a cadence that did not belong to any living community, and could not be translated into neighborly sense no matter how close you leaned.

His face, too, looked oddly mature. He shared his mother’s and grandfather’s lack of chin; yet his firm, precociously shaped nose and the expression in his large, dark, almost Latin eyes gave him an air of quasi-adulthood and an intelligence that seemed more than precocious. Still, he was exceedingly ugly. There was something goatish in the thick lips, the large-pored yellowish skin, the coarse crinkly hair, and the oddly elongated ears. People disliked him more decidedly than they disliked Lavinia and old Whateley. All conjectures about the boy were seasoned with references to the bygone magic of old Whateley—how the hills once shook when he shrieked the dreadful name of Yog-Sothoth within a circle of stones, a great book open in his arms like a cook’s ledger of impossible ingredients.

And the dogs—creatures of pure hearing and honest appetite—abhorred Wilbur. Their barking was not the ordinary complaint at a stranger’s boots. It was a sustained, desperate alarm, a refusal of the ear and nose together. Wherever the boy went, the acoustic peace of farm life—the cluck of hens, the wind in dry corn, the distant knock of an axe—was broken by that harsh canine clamor, as if the countryside itself were trying to warn its people in the only voice it had left. Wilbur, for his part, learned early to take defensive measures against their barking menace, and Dunwich learned, just as early, to listen in spite of itself whenever the dogs began.
